newsitem.title: FRANCE: Scent of victory prompts crush at Socialist rally.
newsitem.headline: Scent of victory prompts crush at Socialist rally.

text.p: Socialist activists were so keen to see their party triumph on Sunday that they overwhelmed security guards to force their way, red roses in hand, into its Left Bank campaign headquarters in Paris.

Less than half an hour before polls closed after the National Assembly runoff and television stations relayed the first projections of results, the gilded iron gates of the Latin American cultural centre, hired for the occasion, were closed to all but media as organisers hurried to ready celebratory drinks and a buffet.

Several hundred militants pressed so hard that they managed to force open the gates and dozens rushed in. Former prime minister Michel Rocard, protesting "Move over, move over", was among those briefly squashed against the gates in the crush.

"On a gagne, on a gagne" (We've won, We've won), they chanted minutes later as the television screen turned red with the Socialist parliamentary victory. The chant was repeated again and again as Socialist Party notables appeared on the monitor during the debate that followed.

Cheers and chants punctuated the evening as activists greeted news of leading centre-right politicians losing their seats. At the defeat of outgoing Justice Minister Jacques Toubon, the cry went up: "Send him to La Sante", a top-security jail in Paris housing politicians tied to corruption probes.

"Chirac resign" was another popular refrain after President Jacques Chirac's gamble in calling a snap election a year early backfired. One reveller commented: "Someone had better watch him tonight otherwise he'll go and hang himself."

One woman who had clutched a red rose, a Socialist symbol much used by the late president Francois Mitterrand, between her teeth for the benefit of photographers said party leader Lionel Jospin had succeeded in embodying resentment not only against premier Alain Juppe but also against Chirac.
"Jospin is modest, he's got new ideas. The lesson for Chirac is clear: either govern with Jospin as prime minister, or resign," said Pierre Casiez, a 34-year-old engineer.
Gregoire van der Elst, a musician in his 30s, said Jospin's key asset had been his honesty and frankness.
"Jospin's campaign had no frills. He was clear on economic issues and on political corruption," he said.

The red roses omnipresent at the victory party were a throwback to the Mitterrand era, but the triumph was vital for the Socialists who had finally managed to turn the page on the legacy of his 14 years in power.
Jospin had come near to achieving the break in the May 1995 presidential election when he earned the tag of "decent loser" for going down in a surprisingly close race with Chirac.
"Jospin has broken with the Mitterrand years. Tonight is the birth of a new Left," said musician van der Elst.
The number of mobile phones used by excited young activists to call their friends from the rally also pointed to a change of generation.

Jospin himself watched the results with his wife in his constituency of Cintegabelle in southwestern France. He looked impassive as campaign workers applauded and cheered the news, noting the results on a slip of paper and allowing himself a wry smile.
